findings.note: TestResultSchemaVersionDistinct's second half cannot prove what its comment claims. The comment (manifest_test.go:107-109) says validation must read ResultSchemaVersion rather than the manifest's own SchemaVersion, and that 'only a result carrying ResultSchemaVersion proves which constant the check uses'. But passingShardResult already sets SchemaVersion: ResultSchemaVersion (manifest_test.go:519), so `fresh.SchemaVersion = ResultSchemaVersion` at line 113 is a no-op assignment and the acceptance loop asserts nothing that TestFreshByShardHash does not already assert. Because SchemaVersion and ResultSchemaVersion are both 1, no test in this file can distinguish the two constants; the comment therefore documents a guarantee the code does not provide, which is worse than an acknowledged gap.

findings.note: The new Go-floor drift check reads go.mod with /^go (\d+\.\d+)$/m (tests/manifest/test-manifests.sh:71), which does not match a patch-qualified go directive. `go 1.26.0` has been legal since Go 1.21 and is what `go mod edit -go=` and some tooling will write, and go.mod's own comment (go.mod:5-14) shows the floor is expected to move. When that happens the check does not report a drift, it throws 'go.mod does not declare a go directive' (line 72) — a message that points the maintainer at a missing directive that is in fact present. Allowing an optional patch segment and comparing on the major.minor pair would fail loudly for the right reason.

evidence.note: regex anchored to exactly two version components
misleading error text on a patch-qualified go directive
current directive is `go 1.26`, which the comment block says is expected to move

findings.note: TestOversizeResultIgnored (manifest_test.go:173) exercises only the over-limit side of the size guard: it builds MaxResultBytes+27 bytes and asserts a non-empty ignore reason. Nothing asserts that a payload at or just under MaxResultBytes still parses, so flipping ParseResult's `>` (internal/reviewmanifest/manifest.go:151) to `>=` — or an off-by-one in the constant — would silently start ignoring legitimate result files with no test failure. Note also that the fixture is not valid JSON (an unterminated string followed by NUL bytes), so the test only demonstrates that the size check runs before json.Unmarshal, not that a large-but-valid result is rejected on size grounds.
